newsitem.title: UK: Tough, unfamiliar market awaits Iraqi oil sales.
newsitem.headline: Tough, unfamiliar market awaits Iraqi oil sales.

text.p: Fierce competition from other oil producers and volatile end-of-year oil markets may make it tougher than expected for Iraq to quickly find buyers for its oil, Western oil traders said.

Rising winter demand in the West should make it easier for Baghdad to place its first oil exports in nearly six years after the U.N. on Monday finally authorised the start of a long-delayed oil-for-food deal.

But a rush to buy at the prices set for December loadings looks unlikely since they are seen as high compared with competiting crudes from Russia and other states in the Middle East, some traders say.
"It's not necessarily going to be easy to sell, particularly to the West. The market structure has changed a lot since 1990," said Bob Finch, head trader at Vitol SA in London.
Turkey, Russia and Romania are expected to be among the first countries to take Iraq's oil, closely followed by France and the United States.
The bulk of the Iraqi exports at first are expected to hit the Mediterranean after being piped from Kirkuk to the Turkish port of Ceyhan.
In the Med, it will meet with stiff competition from Russian, Saudi and Iranian barrels.
Some traders saw Iraqi crude competitively priced against Iranian crude but others said it was expensive compared with Saudi Arabian crudes.
Under the U.N. deal allowing $2 billion worth of sales over six months, Iraq must sell its oil at fair market value.
But hitting a fair price in one of the world's most volatile markets is a difficult balancing act.

In the short-term Italian refiners may be tempted to sign up for Iraqi oil because the main Russian export port of Novorossisk is closed for the next two weeks. But Russian crude is sold on a cargo by cargo basis, which give refiners flexibility while Iraq will only close six month deals.
"It (Iraqi crude) looks attractive compared to Urals (Russian crude) but it isn't nearly as flexible," said a dealer at an independent trading company.

Many European refiners buy most of their crude supplies under yearly contract with Iraq's traditional competitors Saudi Arabia and Iran, who rushed in to fill the void when Baghdad was hit with sanctions in 1990.
Saudi prices are competitive because of a deferred payment clause that allows some refiners to pay up to 40 days after a cargo of crude loads.
Towering backwardation in current oil markets when near-term prices are higher than future prices means that the further forward a refiner buys oil, the cheaper it is.
Increasing market share has also come from the North Sea where production has risen some 35 percent since Iraq was banned from the market.
Refiners enjoy up to 50 days' delay before pricing Saudi crude and have many options to buy short-haul crude from Latin American producers.

Venezuela surpassed Saudi Arabia as the biggest supplier of crude oil to the U.S. last year and increasing exports from Colombia and Mexico have also also muscled in on the world's single largest oil importer.
During the late 1980s, the United States was Iraq's biggest customer, buying more than 500,000 barrels per day in 1990, nearly a third of all Iraq's exports in that year.
Spokesmen for France's Elf Aquitaine and Total, two of the first companies expected to be awarded contracts, said on Monday their firms had not signed deals yet.
The Total spokesman said his company "in principle" is expected to buy 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) but had not finalised the agreement.
Former Iraqi Oil Minister Issam Al-Chalabi, now an industry consultant in Amman, Jordan, doubted whether Iraqi oil exports would resume this month given the various possible logistical problems.

"There is a distinction between pumping and exporting crude...The (companies) who went (to Baghdad) are not signing contracts but confirming an interest, putting final touches and waiting for another round," Chalabi said.
--London newsroom 542 4984
